cards.front: What are the three reasons to nest a class?
cards.back: Grouping classes used in one place, readability, and encapsulation
cards.extra: A helper that only this class needs is better kept inside it than exposed as a second top-level type.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Ex {
  private static class Helper { int n = 1; } // grouped here, readable, hidden
  static void m() { System.out.println(new Helper().n); }
}

cards.front: Which members of the outer class can a static nested class use?
cards.extra: It has no enclosing instance, so instance fields and methods are unreachable without an explicit object reference.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Outer {
  static int shared = 1;
  int instance = 2;
  static class Nested { void show() { System.out.println(shared); /* instance is not accessible */ } }
}

cards.front: Can a static nested class define instance methods and fields?
cards.back: Yes — it can define both static and non-static members
cards.extra: It behaves like a top-level class that happens to be packaged inside another one.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Ex { static class Nested { int value = 7; int twice() { return 2 * value; } }
  static void demo() { System.out.println(new Nested().twice()); } }

cards.front: Which members of the outer class can an inner class use?
cards.back: All of them — static and instance, including private ones
cards.extra: It holds a hidden reference to its enclosing instance, which is exactly what gives it that access.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Outer { private int i = 1; private static int s = 2;
  class Inner { void demo() { i++; s++; System.out.println(i + s); } }
  static void boot() { new Outer().new Inner().demo(); }
}

cards.front: How do you instantiate an inner class?
cards.extra: You cannot create the inner object alone — it must be bound to an enclosing instance at creation.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Outer {
  class Inner { int n = 1; }
  static void m() { Outer outer = new Outer(); Inner i = outer.new Inner(); System.out.println(i.n); }
}

cards.front: What is the one thing an anonymous class cannot do?
cards.back: Declare a constructor — and it cannot extend or implement anything beyond the single type it is created for
cards.extra: It is instantiated at the same moment it is defined, so there is nothing to name and no second use to construct for.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
Runnable r = new Runnable() { // one type only
  public void run() { System.out.println("run"); }
  // Runnable() {} // error: anonymous classes cannot declare constructors
};
r.run();

cards.front: If an inner class declares a field with the same name as the outer's, how do you reach the outer one?
cards.back: Outer.this.field for an instance field, Outer.field for a static one
cards.extra: A bare name resolves to the nearest declaration — the inner class's own. this alone also means the inner instance.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Outer { int field = 1; static int sfield = 2;
  class Inner { int field = 3;
    int read() { return field + Outer.this.field + Outer.sfield; } }
}

cards.front: What must be true for a nested class to be serializable?
cards.back: It must be static, and both it and the enclosing class must implement Serializable
cards.extra: A non-static inner class holds an implicit reference to the outer object, which must then be serializable too — otherwise NotSerializableException.
cards.example:
import java.io.Serializable;
class Ex implements Serializable {
  static class Nested implements Serializable { int n = 1; } // static, both serializable
}
